projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jack Leonard was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: This is Marta Brooks, interviewing Jack Leonard. Today is Monday, April the 7th, 2003. And we are at Jack and Vivian Leonard's home. I appreciate you taking time to do this interview, Jack. I'm going to ask you a couple questions. If you'd first state your full name.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Jack Leonard.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: And your date --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: That's my full name.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: That's your full name. No middle name?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No middle name, no initial, no.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: And then your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: May 6th, 1921.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Great. And then where were you born, Jack?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Salt Lake City, Utah.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Utah. Then can you give me just a little bit about your early life; where you grew up, what it was like?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, I grew up in Salt Lake, right close to Liberty Park. And when I was three years old, the family moved to Portland. And so I grew up in Portland. Went all the way through Sunnyside Elementary School and Washington High School.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Normal growing up, any --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, I had a good time growing up. We had -- that was the Depression. I grew up, obviously, in the middle of the Depression. And so I sold papers downtown when I was twelve, and thirteen, and fourteen. And I worked in the press room at the Oregonian with my dad. And when I graduated from high school, I got a football scholarship and went to Washington D.C. to George Washington University.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: How great.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: And that was a big thing. It was a very valuable scholarship. In today's dollars, that was a hundred thousand dollar scholarship.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Amazing. What were you majoring in?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Business and government.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: And what year was that?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: That was 1940, was when I went back to Washington.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: And a huge thing, during the Depression, too.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Yes. And I planned it.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: You planned it. How did you plan it; what did you do?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: My dad wanted me to work. I had a good job. I had a man's job when I was sixteen. And I could have just stayed right there. And it paid well, and everything was great. And I decided that if I was good in my sports, I could get a college scholarship. And I remember telling the coach after one game -- I did some blocking, the other guy got the touchdown. And he said; well, that was a great play, Jack. I said; well, that's great. All I care about -- I don't care about the touchdown. I care about the scholarship. And he took me with him when he got the job as coach --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: -- at the university. So he took five of us from the northwest back to Washington.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: How long were you in school before you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, we got one year and the war started in Europe. And the draft started. We lost half of our team, half of our squad, got drafted right at the beginning, when the draft first started. And we got the first year. Went back the second year. And I was in the middle of my sophomore year when the Japanese hit Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: So you were drafted or you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No. We all enlisted. We figured we were going to get drafted, so we all enlisted, right, the next -- well, it was interesting. In Washington, everybody was a reserve officer, seemed like. Sunday we were listening to a football game on the radio, University of Oregon was playing Texas and just getting clobbered, eighty to nothing. Anyway, we were listening to the football game, and they broke in with the announcement. And Sunday afternoon -- Monday, when we got up to go to school, the streets were just full of uniforms. Everybody put their uniform on. Because they were automatically called in that -- you know, on Sunday afternoon. They were called in. So I lived in fraternity house. And right downtown in Washington, just a few blocks from the White House. A bunch of us decided that we'd go down and enlist in the Merchant Marine. Because the coach, Bill Reinhart (ph), was going to go up to the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy at King's Point and be the coach up there. So we thought; we've been playing for him and we like him and why don't we go in the Merchant Marine? And it meant getting a commission. So we went down and enlisted.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: So you went into the Merchant Marine?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No. They wouldn't take me.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, I tried. I tried the Air Force -- the Naval Air Corps first. And I had some kind of nasal discharge, and so they wouldn't take me. So I go down, and a bunch of us went down to enlist in the Merchant Marine. And that's fine. We enlisted. We signed all the papers. Now, where's your hometown? Portland, Oregon. Oh, well, you can't go to King's Point. You have to go to San Francisco at Monterey. You have to go to Monterey Academy in San Francisco, which is the Merchant Marine Academy on the west cost. Okay. You're in. You're in. But when you finish this year in school, then you go to Monterey. So okay. I finished the year. I worked at the navy department. The navy department had all kinds of emergency work to do. So they took -- it was just five blocks from the university. It was right there by the university. So they took us down to the main office, down on Constitution Avenue. That was the whole navy department, on Constitution Avenue. And I knew how to type and take shorthand. This old gal who had been in World War I got ahold of me. And oh, boy, she puts me to work in her office.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Do you remember her name at all?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I don't remember her name. Oh, no. I didn't want to remember her name. She was a tiger. Anyway, I worked there till June and decided that I was going to go home. And she said; oh, no. You have to stay here. You're working for the Navy. You can't work anywhere else. You're working for me. And I was doing a good job. And she thought; well, this is great, you know. So I said; no. I'm leaving. She says; you'll never work for the U.S. Government again. I said; okay, and left. But that was an interesting experience. I was working in medical records division there.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: In the Navy?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: In the Navy. And I had all of the medical records in the Navy, from the dates of the Revolutionary War, in the files. We had all of the files all the way back to the Revolutionary War. We can go back and look up John Paul Jones, if we wanted to.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did you ever go back and look?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What did you find out?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Oh, I don't remember now. But we looked up all these interesting people, you know, admirals and captains, important people that had been in the Navy. And we were curious about, gee, what went on. But anyway, I came on home. And I was going to get drafted. I went down to the -- to the Merchant Marine people. And they said; well, yeah. You have to go down to San Francisco. And we can't take you yet. We don't start another class until such and such a date. I had a friend at the draft board -- always been lucky having friends in places. And he called me up and says; hey, your name's coming up. You're going to get drafted. I said; you mean I'm going in the Army as a private? Yeah. What do I have to do? Well, have you enlisted? Yeah, I'm enlisted in the Navy. Okay. Are you in? No. He says; well, you have to be in. I said; what can I do to get in? He says; there's a V-7 program. It's called V-7. V-5, for the Naval Air Corps. And V-7, for the Navy. And if you go down and sign up the papers, and have them sign you in, why, you're all set for another year in school. So I did that. And I got to go back to the University of Oregon for another year. And along with everybody else. We were all reservists of one kind or another.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Had you paid attention then to the war and what's going on?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Oh, amen, yeah.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: On the radio?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Every day, we watched the paper. Remember, that was 1942, was the bad year. That was when Japan took the Philippines. They went all through southeast Asia, China, Singapore, Midway, which was the turnaround. And all of the advance -- and we'd follow the paper every day. They'd color the pictures to show what the Japanese -- where they were, down to Guadacanal. And so then in July, I went to -- we were all called in, sworn in. And I went to UCLA as an enlisted man, as an apprentice seaman for the -- we had to wait to get in midshipman school. They could only handle a thousand at Notre Dame and a thousand at Columbia, and they could only handle a thousand at Northwestern. That was all they could handle for the four months training period, for your commission. So we had to wait until next class opened up. So I was at UCLA from July till October, 1942. And that was -- that was a big experience. I had a great time. We were in uniform in Los Angeles, UCLA.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Perfect.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Went to -- went down to the Stagedoor Canteen. Dick Powell picked us up, another guy and I.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Leonard
sp.p: She wouldn't remember.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: I do. I remember Dick Powell.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Dick Powell, big name. You bet. He picked us up on the street. We were just walking along. He stopped his car, had another band member with him. Says; where are you going? Stagedoor Canteen. So am I, get in. Took us in. There's a line of a thousand or fifteen hundred guys waiting to get in. He takes us in the back door, and we didn't have to stand in line. And we stayed in -- they'd let you go in for an hour, and then you had to leave. Because they had all those people waiting. He took us in, said; you can stay as long as you'd like. He was just being nice. Because he felt -- you know, like a lot of guys. He was home. We were going. There were a lot of people there then who had been at Guadacanal and been hurt or had put in a long tour, and they were back home. So those were the people that he -- I think he got us mixed up. But we were just a couple of kids. That was Art Hosfeld (ph),honey. That was Art. Yeah. So we had a wonderful time. We met people, Hollywood people. They invited us out to the studio. So the next weekend, we went to a studio, and we sat at the top of the stairs. They were filming the Sweetheart of Sigma Chi. Marsha Hunt was in it, and her dad was a Sigma Chi. He invited us down to the office. He was the internal revenue commissioner for southern California, and he was a Sigma Chi. And he treated us just like royalty. So we got to go to the studio and sit on the set, and had a great time. But after we got through our semester -- which was what we were allowed, because we were coming up seniors. And we were sent back to Norfolk, another two-month waiting period. And I was put in charge of the train. We had a special train taking all of the reservists from that area. And I took a train of sailors from Los Angeles to Norfolk.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: How many were in your group, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. A hundred, hundred fifty. A few cars. And it was awful. We didn't have any heat. We didn't have any food. We didn't have any bunks. And it was a five -- let's see, it was a six-day trip.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, we just -- we suffered. We went across Texas. And it was November, and it was cold. And, oh, I was in charge. And I remember when we finally got to Cincinnati, Ohio, I told a guy; we got to do something. Boy, we're suffering. He said; all right. We'll park out here for a little while, for a day or two. And you can do whatever you do. That's up to you. But you be on those cars ready to go at such and such a time. So I took all the guys down to the YMCA. And they all got showers, and they got to run around town. And I told them; if you don't get back and if you aren't here when it's time to go, you aren't going to get a commission. And not one guy missed it.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: They all come back.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: And got back on the cars, back on the train. And they hooked us up to another train and took us into Norfolk.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What happened when you got to Norfolk?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, we spent two months there. And they had a training program. And I was an instructor in the training program; (Guts). Just all the stuff that -- and Portsmouth is a big Navy yard. And so we got to go on the ships, and got an indoctrination in shipboard.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Now, had you been trained in this prior to this?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: So how did you become a instructor?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I just got picked.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Read the manual?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Somebody back in UCLA said; use this guy. So I got used.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Lucky. In December, we went to Columbia, to midshipman school. We were there for four months, in New York. And then we were commissioned. And in New York, we had leave. We were free every weekend. Had a marvelous time. Went to church. Does that count?

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Yeah. I think so.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, that was before there was any real (Hackney) group in New York. We used to meet in -- oh, now, I forgotten the name of it. Viv, help me out. The hall, name of the piano. What's the big --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Leonard
sp.p: Steinway Hall.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Steinway Hall. Met in Steinway Hall.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: And this is the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: This is the Church of Jesus Christ, Latter Day Saints. And that was the branch for Manhattan. That was all. That was it. There were about, oh, thirty or forty of us. And I met some people that I'd known in Washington, who had worked for Mariott. And we went to Sunday school and church together in Washington. And they were working in New York. One of them -- one girl was the secretary for the commanding general of New York area. So we had -- we had a real interesting time. We could -- we met people and we did things and got commissioned. And at the end of training, we had interviews. We had an opportunity to request duty, whatever we were interested in. So these guys came up and they were interviewing for an outfit called Scouts and Raiders. And John Bell was --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Leonard
sp.p: See his picture here?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Yeah, he was in charge. And Bob Harrick (ph), was his executive officer. And they were very impressive.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Impressive, as, what do you mean?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: The way they explained what they were planning to do. They had been in North Africa. It's all in the book there, if you want to look at it later. But they were recruiting for people to -- this was the first attempt to organize people to act as advance scouts for the Navy. Navy had never done anything like this before. And as a result of the campaigns at Tarawa and Kwajalein, it was recognized -- Admiral King recognized that there were going to be some problems. And they were getting ready for North Africa, which was the first landings in Europe. And so they had taken a group of Navy chiefs who were football coaches and pro football players, and people with athletic backgrounds, and physically able to do what they needed to do. What they planned to do was send them in, in advance of the landing force. So that they could get the landing craft to the right place, to the right beach, to the right wharf, and so on. And they had all done that. North Africa was all over. They were getting ready for -- let's see if I get my dates straight. This is February, March, 1943. '42 to '43 -- no. 1944. February, March, 1944. And Normandy was all over. In fact, most of the campaign in Europe was pretty well along. And they were getting ready for the Pacific. They -- give me my little book. I've got some markings here. We were scheduled to go -- I volunteered. They gave us a -- they tried to -- tried to scare everybody out. And we were selected. There were quite a large number who volunteered. We were thirty out of -- well, there was a class of over a thousand. And probably a hundred and fifty volunteered. A lot of guys did not want to be on a transport. They didn't want to be on amphibious duty. That was sort of the bottom rung of the ladder. Everybody wanted to be on a PT boat. Well, that was all taken. We had all the PT boats that they needed, and so on, and so on. Anyway, this looked like an opportunity to not have to be held accountable for everything that we did -- can you turn it off for a second? (Tape is turned off.)

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Okay. Jack, can you describe some of the things that you were trained to do then?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, what we were designed -- what the organization was designed for was to accomplish the primary missions of scouting, beach marking, attacking areas, in remote areas, doing anything that would be done in advance of a major operation. And the organization was the outgrowth of previous, prior operations. Started at North Africa, and they -- Eric, Bell, Brewster -- there was a whole crew of about seven or eight officers, all received Navy Crosses at North Africa, and then another group at Normandy. They came back to train us to do the same thing in the Pacific. And the problem in the Pacific was entirely different than the North Atlantic. So what they needed were people who could be able, physically, to go without sleep, swim --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Endure, yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: -- anything that needed to be done. The training was the same training -- we were the pioneers of all of the -- a book written -- a book written by Kevin Dockery entitled, SEALS In Action, explains that the Scouts and Raiders were the prelude to underwater demolition teams. All of the training that they did, physical training that came to be known as the (Buds) program, was developed by Scouts and Raiders, who they trained UDT teams how to do it.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: You described that you're in New York at this time?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Where are you taking this?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: They had been selected, and we were sent to Ft. Pierce, Florida. And there was a big story about how it got to be -- how the training base got to be Ft. Pierce. Admiral King was insistent that it be in an area where they could have good facilities, and there weren't any in Florida at the time. But they wanted warm water and they wanted good weather, and they didn't want to be up in New England someplace where it was going to be miserable and couldn't do anything outside. So they traveled up and down the east coast of Florida. And they finally found this spot at Ft. Pierce, which was totally isolated. It's a -- kind of a lagoon. It's marshes and swamp, and the most miserable place in the world. In fact, it was a research station for mosquito control. And poisonous snakes, alligators, everything under the sun to make life miserable. And that was the spot they picked.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did you regret volunteering after this?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, the first -- the first month we darn near died. If was awful. We were in tents on the beach, sand fleas. We were up all night, and couldn't sleep in the heat and the daytime. And had to train during the day. And it was the most grueling, difficult, physical training that you can imagine.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Can you describe -- do you remember, like, a day? What would a day be like?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, we'd get through maybe two, three, four o'clock in the morning, because we were out doing things all night, slogging around in the mud, swimming in the ocean, coming in to the beach to try to sneak past the instructors who were acting as sentries and so on. And we'd do this till -- if we were lucky and we got in, we got past them, then we'd get in and we'd get some sleep. But if we got caught, then we had to go out and do it all over again. And sometimes we'd get in at three or four o'clock in the morning. Then we were up again at seven, eight. They'd get us up. We had to run up and down the beach a couple of miles. Then we'd use five hundred or six hundred pound -- big palm tree logs, and six guys to a log, and you did exercises with the logs. And you had to do them together. Because if you got out of sync, you got rapped on the head with a log. So it was real interesting, real interesting thing. And we did small arms, all the stuff -- small boats. Everything that the SEALS later developed for Vietnam was pioneered at Ft. Pierce.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What kept you going?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: The group, pride. Nobody going to wash out. You're not going to be the guy that doesn't make it. The SEALS have discovered that people can do ten times more than they thought they could, just because -- they're just not going to give up. They're going to keep on going. And it's -- it's -- everybody doesn't make it. We -- we got through the training. We didn't lose anybody, because we were -- well, in the first place, we were a selected group. We didn't have any enlisted men, to begin with. And we got through the training. And then we were supposed to get enlisted men. By that time, there was a lot of political maneuvering going on between Lieutenant Commander Kauffman, who was really the founder, the original commanding officer of underwater demolition teams. He was the son of Admiral Kauffman, and he had some clout. So gradually the UDT teams took precedence, because they were designed to engage in demolition work, which was what they were going to do. And that was needed, because of the discovery of all of the -- what's the word I want -- obstacles, to the beaches. And they had to be blown up. They had to -- and this had started back in North Africa and in Europe. They had a history. Scouts, Raiders were first, and then the UDTs came along. And then they were combined. And ultimately, they ended up with our group. We were -- we were in Class 6 at Ft. Pierce for Scouts, Raiders. We were sent to advanced Naval intelligence school in New York for six weeks. And the UDT teams were sent to Maui, and set up a base in Maui. That became the UDT headquarters for the rest of the war. And our group ended up going to Pearl Harbor after we finished the intelligence training. And we were given a choice. We could --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: We could stay in the intelligence group, or we could go with the underwater demolition group.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: So do you remember the date that you got to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: We got to Pearl Harbor -- let's see. July, August, October -- October, November. November, 1944.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What do you remember about Pearl Harbor? Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: When we got to Pearl Harbor, we came individually. No. We went to San Diego. We went from New York to San Diego to the amphibious training base in Coronado. And we had to wait there for transportation. Then we were put on a ship, and we sailed to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Do you remember the name of your ship?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No. It was a -- I do remember the ship. It was a Danish luxury liner.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Oh, that's nice.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: That had been converted to a troop transport. It had a huge big deck, promenade deck. And we played volleyball. Oh, we had a great time. Eight days from San Diego to Honolulu to Pearl Harbor. And we had a great time. Marvelous food. Just a great trip. We thought, man, this is -- we made a right choice.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Well, after Ft. Pierce, that was --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Did the right thing. Ft. Pierce was just hell. It was just awful. And a lot of it was because there was a -- a feeling of ambivalence about whether we were ever really going to do what we were training to do. Because there was no big land mass, except China -- well, we weren't -- we were hopping over islands. This was after -- the Philippines were under way. We were too late for the Philippines. And the big operation that was coming up was Iwo. And there wasn't going to be anything that we were trained to do on Iwo, because there it was, five miles long and a three-knot curve. And -- so anyway, we didn't know what we were going to do. I opted to stay in the intelligence group. We got to Pearl Harbor, and it was -- it was pretty well established. Most of the repairs had all been done. The war -- we knew we were going to win. By this time, the middle of 1944, we were -- Halsey, Nimitz, MacArthur. We were at the Philippines, and we were on the way to Japan. It was just a question of how long it would take and how many would die on the way. So we were indoctrinated. We went to classes. I volunteered for minesweepers. This is an advanced force. And I was assigned to commander mine pack, Admiral Alexander U.S. Sharp. He was an old admiral who had been commandant of the east coast. And he wanted to see shipboard, like he never been -- (The whole side of Tape 1, Side 1, just went blank right here.) END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE MS. BROOK:

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did he use his influence?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: -- to get a command at sea. So he got the command of all the minesweepers and mine layers in the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Why did you decide this, to do the mine -- that's very dangerous.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Somebody -- I just thought, well, you know, got to do something. I had decided that the UDT operation was sort of a dead end, and it looked like there would be more of an opportunity to do something with -- with an attack force, do what we'd been trained to do. At the intelligence school, we were -- we were trained to be advance intelligence officers. And there hadn't been any intelligence officers in the Navy. And that's kind of an interesting story. When I reported to the flagship, Admiral Sharp -- the operations officer was Captain Clark. And I went in. I was taken in to him by the aide and introduced to him. He says; what are you supposed to do? And I explained to him. I had a tin box with the operation order. I had all of the -- all of the material that he had, in my tin box, I'm carrying around. And I said; well, I've been trained as an intelligence officer. And we can brief people on what they're going to do. Look, I don't need anybody to tell me what's going on. Get that man off this ship. Later I found out that he thought we were being assigned to look for homosexuals in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Huh.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: That's what he -- his own personal feeling.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Interpretation of that.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Which was just a big joke. I don't know where he ever got that idea. I don't know what --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Anyway, it was just a big mistake. And -- but he kicked me off the ship. So I go back to John Fox, who was in charge of all the intelligence group, for Admiral Turner. And Admiral Turner was the -- in charge of the amphibious operations in the Pacific. He was one step below Nimitz. And -- so Fox was right there with Turner. And we were there because Turner had sent us there. And this had come up before. And he said; go on back. So I go back. He says; oh, send him over to the Gamble. Sent him over to Clay, Captain Clay on the Gamble. And so I was assigned the Gamble, which was an old (DE). Had been in World War I, and it was a mess. And so I'm over there. And he figures I'm out of his hair and out of the way. So we got ready, and we left Pearl to go to Iwo. And I'm -- oh, I've got -- I'm in miserable shape. I don't have a regular bunk. I'm just -- you know, I'm not assigned to the ship. I'm assigned to count mine packs. So I'm sleeping over the rudder.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did they feed you?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: And they let me eat, yeah. And Clay was the commander, Naval Academy guy from Annapolis. And he thought; gee, this is great. I've got my own private intelligence officer. So he put me to work on cryptography and communications, which was all right. But we go to Iwo. We get two days out, a freighter, APA, has to come back, because they've got trouble. We're assigned to take it back to Pearl. I get back to Pearl. They're not going to take you. They take me off the Gamble. Fox sends orders down. Take me off the Gamble, and put me on a plane, and fly me out to Guam, with my box and all my materials. And when I get out there, I'm to report to Commander Freiburghouse -- I just remember his name, because it's such an unusual name, on the U.S.S. Challenge. And I knew this, because I had all the orders. And I knew everything that was going on. So I knew that he was going to be the lead ship in Iwo. So I got on board, and we left to go to Iwo. We sailed into Iwo three days before the landings.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What was the date, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I don't remember the date. I've got it written down somewhere's. But it was three days. D-minus three. And we sailed in. And I had a little Vargus camera. My assignment -- I had dreamed up for myself. I was going to look at the beaches. I knew all the information we had -- and this is another story. We had no information about any of the islands in the Pacific prior to the landing. That's why Tarawa was such a mess, that's why Kwajalein was such a disaster. We didn't know about the corral reefs. There was one Australian yachtsman who had sailed up in that area in the years prior to the war, back in the thirties, late twenties. And he had come to Pearl Harbor and met with Nimitz. He was the single source of information about those islands. And that was one reason why our group had been organized in the first place. So anyway, we -- we got to Iwo. And there it was, and we sailed in, lead ship. I got to stand on the bridge. We got to look at Iwo without anything else in front of us. We were the first ones there. And I knew what was there, where the guns were and everything. Set up -- no mines to sweep, because the current's too heavy, too strong. And it turned out -- I found out later -- we didn't know this. But there was a UDT team coming up behind us. And they got there the next day after we did. And one of the fellows that I met at the end of the -- after the Okinawa campaign, swam in to a little rock off the north end of the island and hung on to that rock about eighteen hours in that current, cold water. And he hung on to that rock. And he was there, in case -- just in case something came in. He was sort of like a lighthouse on that rock. Marvelous.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Courage.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Courage, what he did.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Do you remember his name?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I don't remember his name. I didn't -- I only knew him for a day. He was -- I was with the UDTs for the -- what was going to be the invasion of Japan. But that's another story. That's later. So anyway, I watched the whole operation at Iwo. There wasn't anything for me to do. I'm on this little minesweeper. And here they're coming in with this armada of ships. And I'm sitting there, we're sailing around the island. At the second day, we're sailing around the north end. And they don't shoot at us. Why? We can't hurt them. Obviously, we're not landing. So we're sailing. And they don't fire at us. We went in so close that I could see the faces of the Japanese soldiers. I could see the tunnels on Mt. Sorimachi. And the tragedy was, I could not see the implacements of five-inch guns that they had put above the berm of the beach. They built concrete implacements, and they camouflaged them, and I didn't see them. Well, we got in close. And on the third day -- first day of the landing, landing crafts are out. And we're sailing in between and in and around. And they start firing these five-inch guns. And I'm right there, and I could see them. And I tried to send a message to -- well, first -- first -- two days before I tried to send the message to the Commander Blandy -- no -- yeah. Blandy, Admiral Blandy, that the beaches looked soft. They were black lava sand, and they looked real soft. They were large pebbles. And it was going to be a mess for track vehicles. And Freiburghouse wouldn't even break radio silence. Says we can't do that until the day of the landing. They should see us. We're sailing around the island, see. But he wouldn't send it. So it didn't get sent. And the track vehicles all got bogged down and clogged the exits to the beach, which was too bad. The one time we had a chance to do something and it didn't get done. But I watched the whole landing. I took pictures. They fired star shells over the island, and they had Iwo lit up like daylight. And I sent all the film over to the flagship, and I never saw it again.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: They kept it, or you don't know if they lost it, or --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know whether it was any good. But I never saw it again. But I had pictures of the boats going into the landing, on the beaches. There was a beach on the southeast side, and a beach on the northwest side. As I recall, the island was like this. And the landing beach was here, and Sorimachi was here, and another beach -- the alternate beach was there. And so after fifteen days, why, it was more or less -- the island wasn't secured. But the landing that was secured, the forces were on the beach and there wasn't anything for us to do. So we were sent back to Guam -- Saipan. I can't remember whether it was Saipan or Guam. We were sent back. And captain, the ship's captain -- well, that's the end of it for me. He says; I've only got orders to take you to Iwo. And he puts me on the beach. And my orders are to commander mine pack, Pacific. Commander mine pack is in Ulithi. I'm in Saipan, on the beach. And I can't get anything to eat. I can't get a place to sleep. I'm -- I'm sitting there at this makeshift airport, you know, this landing field. And this is -- this is a few months after Saipan has been secured. There's still Japanese out there, see. And I can't get off the island. I'm stuck there. And I'm in there, and I'm sitting there. And in comes Commander Clay. His ship, the Gamble, that I was on --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: -- was sunk.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: They took a bomb. A Japanese plane flew down. And that was probably the only casualty, Naval casualty, of the whole landing. There was one cruiser that was hit, off the north end of the island. I was going to mention that. We were sailing right around, and they hit the cruiser. Not us. They didn't bother even shooting at us. But they hit the cruiser. But that was -- those were the only Naval casualties of bigger ships, other than amphibious craft. There was one thing about the landings that I didn't mention. Those landing crafts, the LCIs, came into the beach. Those big guns on the beach just blew them out of the water. Wiped them out.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Huge casualties.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Big losses. The Terror was the flagship for Admiral Sharp. And later when I got on board the Terror, they told me, they went around and they just threw a (board) over the ship and tow it out, tow it back out. And tried -- all they could do is take off the bodies. Some of those ships, they only had about five-man crews. But they had a hundred and fifty men. And they had maybe eight, ten, fifteen --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Left, right?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: -- people who weren't casualties.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Do you remember how you felt? I mean, that would be the first time you'd seen a combat, right?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: That was terrible. That was tough. Because there wasn't anything we could do. All we could do was watch. And we knew -- by this time, we knew -- we might as well been in Madison Square Garden or ball grounds, playing ball. Because we were just there, and watching. There wasn't anything we could do. We weren't big enough to help anybody. And we didn't have any guns. I mean, mine crafts don't have anything to shoot with. And so we were just there, basically spectators, watching the landings at Iwo. The Japanese had one plane. One plane got off the runway and up in the air, on the first day, and was shot down before it got five hundred feet up in the air. Anyway, we got --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did you do some self-talk? What did you do? I mean, you've seen this now. You just have orders, and so you --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I get back to Saipan, and Clay comes in and rescues me. He says; gee, whiz. What are you going to do? I said; I'm got to get back to the Terror somehow. My orders are to Sharp. I can't go to anybody -- nobody else will accept me. They won't even give me anything to eat over here. He says; come on. I'll take you with me. He was a good guy. He had sense enough to understand that I was -- I was stranded, in serious shape. I didn't have any outfit. I didn't have any ship. So he took me down to Ulithi -- Falalop atoll, at Ulithi. And that was the staging area for the operation at Okinawa. There were probably fifteen hundred ships there. It was a huge lagoon. And you can put fifteen hundred ships there. It was twenty miles across. And we get down there. We go, like, over to the Terror, which is out in the lagoon. I managed to get -- Clay let me take a boat and I got over to the Terror. I go up. Captain Clark, go in his office. Get that man off this ship.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: He didn't like you much.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: He didn't want me on the ship. And he sent me to the beach. And there wasn't anything there -- well, there was a nice quonset hut. I had a quonset hut all to myself, twenty bunks, clean. Clean sheets every day if I wanted them. Sleep in a different bunk every day. Good officers' club. Good food.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: And I could have stayed right there the rest of the war. That would have been -- he would have been happy.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: This was because they didn't know what to do with you, because of the special training?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: He didn't want me on the ship, because he didn't have any idea what I was supposed to do, what I was trained for. And this -- this is all -- this book on the SEALS, and the book on the Scouts, Raiders. There were lots of instances of that. That happened in Normandy. That happened at Normandy. The Scouts and Raiders and underwater demolition people who were sent to Normandy were combined with other groups and weren't allowed to do what they were supposed to do.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Was it because it was not communicated well --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: -- systemically through the branches --

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Well, the orders didn't get passed out. This originated -- this all started right at the top with King and Turner. And -- and the admirals and officers in charge of subordinate groups simply didn't know about this. There wasn't any way to get the information to them. And unless Kauffman was able to do it, because his father was an admiral, he can call him on the phone and say; dad, how can I do this. Or; what can I do to get through, or something. General Baldwin had a meeting -- it's in the book. General Baldwin had a meeting with Nimitz, oh, first part of '44, 1944. And explained how he wanted to combine his Office of Strategic Services, the OSS, with the fighting forces in the Pacific. Because their work was pretty much done, what they can do, in Europe. And he knew -- he recognized that there was going to be a real problem in the Pacific theater. So they did that. And then this is where the story gets kind of interesting. Because -- Captain Clark comes over to the beach, to the officers' club. Well --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Your quonset hut?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: In the quonset hut. I'm laying in the quonset hut one night. All of a sudden they're shooting, all around. A bunch of guys, a bunch of sailors were attacking the officers' club. Because there was a hospital ship in the lagoon. The nurses were all over at the officers' club. The senior officers were all over at the officers' club. And the sailors on the beach found out about it, and there was gunfire. Oh, it was a real mess. And this was the sort of thing that nobody ever wrote up, nobody ever heard about. I'm laying in that quonset hut on the floor, wondering if I'm going to get shot by some stray bullet. Anyway, that was an interesting experience. And I had one other experience. Turn it off. (Tape is turned off.)

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: You can't go anyplace?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Can't go anyplace.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Been shot at?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Did we record about the -- yeah, okay. So there I am. And that's all over with. So I asked the commodore if we can have a church service -- if I can put out a message, if there's any Latter Day Saints. And I'm not a, what do we call it? I'm not a special --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Leonard
sp.p: Not a chaplain.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Group leader. I'm not a chaplain, by any stretch. But I wasn't an assigned group leader, or anything like that. So I asked him if he'd invite anybody to come in and we'd have church service. So he did. He put out the message. Seven guys come in, soaking wet. They had a little boat, you know. Come from a destroyer or from a landing craft or something. And seven guys come in. One of them was a member -- sort of a golden prospect. His friend, his buddy, was teaching him the Gospel. And they came in, and we had church service there in this nice little quonset chapel that they had. And I was in charge. I was the only officer in the group. And I organized -- so I -- I didn't know what to do.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did you have sacrament?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I had my Book of Mormon, and my Bible. My little military -- Faust, elder Faust mentioned this in his conference. Well, I had my little military books. And so we -- we organized. We had the sacrament. And we had our little testimony -- and in the middle of our testimony meeting, we just had this marvelous manifestation. We knew -- we were jumping up and down, we were hugging each other, we were laughing, we were crying. We had a real manifestation with the Holy Ghost. And I knew, we all knew, we weren't going to be harmed. We were going to be all right. That was what we were told. We were going to be safe. And it was just marvelous. And we had -- I had -- we were so excited and so enraptured with this experience, we didn't get any names, we didn't get any addresses. We didn't get anything. They had to go back to their ship. They only were allowed an hour, hour and an a half, two hours to be away. And they had to go ten miles across the lagoon. And so they -- they left, and then there I was, all alone again. But we had that marvelous experience.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: What an assurance that must have been for you to go on then.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: About two days later, Captain Clark comes into the officers' club, gets dead drunk. The seaman who bring him in the boat, come over to me. They know I'm there. This is all over the ship, see. They come over to me, say; what are we going to do? They won't let us in the club. He won't come out. Can you do anything?

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Your quonset hut.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: I said; well, I'll try. I'll try. I was willing to do whatever I could do. So I go over to the officers' club. And boy, he was dead drunk. And picked him up, took him out. I brought the sailors in, thinking, we took Clark out, put him in the boat, took him back to the ship. I'm out on the ship. What am I going to do? He's drunk. He's in the bunk. So the next morning, they take me back to the beach. I'm back in my quonset hut. And a couple of sailors show up. Come on out to the ship, the Admiral wants to see you again. And the Admiral -- he don't remember. He talked to me. We had a nice conversation. I explained to him why I was there. Gave him the whole story. And he said; well, we'll find you a bunk. We got a place for you. And he says; do you know anything about communications? I says; oh, yeah, yeah. I worked with Commander Clay on the communications. Oh, okay. Yeah, all right. So he puts me in the communications section. And I had a nice stateroom. There were six of us in a big, big stateroom. The Terror was a converted cruiser. It was converted into a flagship. And it had all of the amenities. We had ice cream, we had baked Alaska, we had steak, we had everything. I had hot chocolate prepared for me by a mess man. And so the Admiral told me that I would work for him, and I was his assistant. He had an old guy in his fifties. I'm twenty-five -- twenty-four. I'm twenty-four years old. Twenty-three. I'm twenty-three years old. And so I'm working in communications and on an ECM. An ECM is a cryptography machine, like a typewriter, decode messages. So I'm doing that. I'm cleared. I got clearance. And I show him my box. I still got my tin box with the operation order in it. I got the operation order that he's got. And that's impressive, see. Turner had provided us with all of the means to impress these people so that we can do what we were supposed to do. So I'm drawing maps and I'm getting ready to brief all of the minesweeper personnel and all this sort of thing. And the Admiral comes down -- or he sends a guy down and takes me up. And; what do you know about this traffic? He says; I can't break it. And the communications officer for the staff was there. And he's a commander. I'm an ensign. But I'll tell you what. I'm talking to a -- who had been a three-star Admiral commander in the whole east coast. And I say; Admiral Turner told us that if we ever ran into something that we couldn't handle, that if we got to him, we'd get some help. Oh. I'm going to a meeting on the El Dorado in about a day or two and he'll be there. I'm going to take you with me. His whole staff -- see, he's got twenty people on his staff there, all captains, captains. So we get ready, we go out, get on his barge. Oh, fancy. You know, the macrame, the mahogany. Fancy. And we get in this barge and go up to the El Dorado. And up the gangway, up the ladder. We get up, officer of the deck, three-star Admiral and an ensign. And he says; okay. Tell him what you told me. So I told him. He says; oh. Well, I'll get Commander so-and-so. And so he goes. And gets -- turns out, that he gets the communications officer for Admiral Turner. And he comes down, and Sharp says -- he's a very imposing man. He's a big man, about 6, 2; 6, 3. Gray hair, big, and very Admiralish. A typical Admiral. And he says; he's with me. Talk with him. And so I tell him what he said. Oh, okay. So he takes the Admiral, and they go and talk to Admiral Turner. And they come back. The commander comes back, when they're all through with their conference -- I wait there, oh, I don't know, an hour, two hours. I wait there. They got a -- you know, it's a deck area, the fan tail of the ship, where all the boats come, that are coming and going. And the El Dorado is a huge ship. That is big AP, fifteen hundred people on it. And -- well, maybe not that many. Maybe a thousand. Communications gear. This is the flagship for a landing operation. They'll know. Anyway, after about an hour and a half or two hours, they come back. The commander hands me a folder. And he says; this is the key to the Oki traffic. And we're talking -- just the two of us. The officer of the deck, on the other side of the fan tail. And he says; I'm giving -- to the Admiral standing there; I'm giving this to you, and you're signing for it, not him. If anything happens to it, you're the one that goes to Leavenworth. The Oki traffic was the communications dealing with material that came from the broken codes. It was the most secret information that we had. They wouldn't give it to the Admiral, supposedly. But Turner recognized -- you know, Sharp is senior to Turner. And all they were doing was making -- you know, making me the guy that was going to handle -- the Admiral's going to take care of it. I'm the fall guy. But they weren't worried about that. But he was -- what he was doing was sending the message to all the people on his staff; we set up these programs and we expect you to use them. These people are trained. And it was very impressive to them that we had been through the Scout and Raider training. That's what I never told him to put in his book, see. It would have been good for everybody in the program, everybody who went through that miserable, lousy, rotten training at Ft. Pierce. Somebody actually got to the top rung --

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: And made a statement?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: -- and was rewarded. Turner meant it when he said it. He gave me the key to the Oki traffic.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Yeah, trust.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: And I went back to the ship with the Admiral and we talked on the way back, and he was just real nice. And he says; this is what you're going to do.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: Did he ever apologize?

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Oh, no. Oh, no. He didn't have anything -- that wasn't his fault. He didn't know anything about it. Clark had done that. And Clark was a great man. He was really a great man. I never blamed him or held anything against him. Because he was out there. He could have gone back to Pearl where his wife was any time he wanted to. He could have gone, got on a plane, written his own orders, gone back to Pearl, seen his wife for a couple days, and got back on the ship. He never left. He never left the forward area. He was a great man. And subesequently -- I'll explain -- he got killed.

Anyway, we go back to the ship. I had my own office. I had my own ECM. I had my own setup. I got the Oki traffic. I'm in charge of the Oki traffic. And I'm breaking this material as it comes in. So that Sharp knows what's going on all over the Pacific ocean area. This is the -- the name (ultra), was top secret. We couldn't mention that. Nobody on the ship knew that we had it. We're all ready, training's all done. They're all ready to go to Okinawa. So the advance landing force. Sharp's in command. He's got, I don't know, three hundred ships. I've got all the operation order, I've got all the intelligence material. I've got everything in my tin box, and we're ready to go. We go out to sea. And the second night out, one of the seamen, one of the staff, enlisted men come out. Admiral wants you up in the office. So I go up. He says; you've got the watch tonight. How are we doing for time? It's eight o'clock already.

sp.speaker: Marta Brooks
sp.p: We're good. I know this is going to end in just one second, so I want to make sure I get the whole story. So you had the watch.

sp.speaker: Jack Leonard
sp.p: Okay. And I'd never stood deck watch in my life. I don't know anything about running a ship. I don't know about communications, innership communications. I don't know anything. And I'm up there. And it's the midwatch. It's midnight, midnight to four o'clock. And what do I do? Well, it's dark. Things are going on, but I don't have to do anything. The ship is running. I know all the people on the ship. We got acquainted by now. And so I'm standing around, looking like I --
[END OF INTERVIEW]
